summary: Describes an IANA-maintained registry for IETF standards that use XML-related items such as namespaces, DTDs, schemas and RDF schemas. It is a best current practice document and sets up where those names get recorded.

eli5.summary: A big notebook lists each XML name used in Internet standards so no two groups pick the same one. This explains how that notebook works and who writes in it.

questions: how to register an xml namespace with iana
what is the ietf xml registry
what are the xml registry classes
subtitle: An IANA-run registry that gives XML namespaces, DTDs and schemas used in IETF standards a stable, unique name.

tldr.problem: Several IETF standards defined XML DTDs, namespaces and schemas, and some simply made up non-resolvable URIs to name them, with no authoritative place to look them up.
tldr.mechanism: IANA keeps a registry of XML items, assigns URNs of the form urn:ietf:params:xml:CLASS:ID on request, and stores the registered document. Specifications ask for entries with a short template in their IANA considerations section.
tldr.outcome: XML identifiers in IETF standards get one authoritative home. The registry works on a First Come First Served basis, but a specification is required.

facts.label: Policy
facts.value: First Come First Served, Specification Required

today: RFC 3688 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 81). The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the document that defines the IETF XML registry.

sections.title: Why an XML Registry
sections.content:
RFC 3688 describes an IANA-maintained registry for IETF standards that use XML-related items: namespaces, Document Type Declarations (DTDs), schemas and Resource Description Framework (RDF) schemas. The document is a Best Current Practice.

The motivation is practical. Several IETF working groups had produced standards defining DTDs, XML Namespaces and XML Schemas, and each of these identifies things with URIs. Some standards skipped PUBLIC identifiers in favour of 'well known' SYSTEM identifiers, which proved to be more trouble than they were worth. The result was that several IETF standards simply created non-resolvable URIs just to identify, not resolve, the DTD for a given XML document.

The registry gives document authors and implementors an authoritative location for their XML elements. IANA maintains the public representation of the document, the URI for the element if one is provided at registration, and a registry of Public Identifiers as URIs. If the registrant does not ask for a particular URI, IANA assigns a URN that follows RFC 3553.
sections.eli5: People kept inventing names for their XML files that nobody could look up. This RFC creates one official list so everyone can find the real name.

sections.title: The Assigned URI
sections.content:
Every element in the registry, except PUBLIC identifiers, needs a URI. A registrant who wants one assigned gets a URN of the form urn:ietf:params:xml:<class>:<id>. The <class> is the type of document being registered, and the <id> is a unique id generated by IANA by any means it deems necessary to keep it unique and persistent.

There is a condition: for such a URN to be assigned, the item MUST have been through the IETF consensus process, which basically means it is documented in an RFC.

IANA also maintains a file server, reachable by at least HTTP and FTP, holding all the registered elements. The RFC suggests organizing files by <class>, with the <id> as the file name, but the directory structure is up to IANA.

Implementors are warned not to rely programmatically on those resources being available or on the directory structure staying static. Some tools download DTDs and schemas on the fly, and developers should not treat IANA as a 'schema download repository'. This is why IANA does not register or provide SYSTEM identifiers.
sections.eli5: The registry hands out a name tag in a fixed pattern. But it is a name tag, not a download shelf, so your program should not keep running to the library for a copy every time.

sections.title: The Four Registerable Classes
sections.content:
The registry accepts four classes of XML item. Each one gets its own kind of URN.

  • publicid: a PUBLIC identifier, a name meant to be meaningful across systems. It must use only the public identifier characters from the XML 1.0 specification, so a URN can serve as one. If the registrant gives none, IANA assigns one of the form urn:ietf:params:xml:pi:<id>. SYSTEM identifiers are system-specific, so they are not registered.
  • ns: an XML namespace, which is named by a URI and has no machine-parseable representation. The registered document is the specification or a reference to it. IANA assigns urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:<id> if no URI is given.
  • schema: an XML Schema, which is also identified by a URI but is machine parseable. The registered document is the schema file, and the assigned URN is urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:<id>.
  • rdfschema: an RDF schema, whose grammars about relationships between URIs are identified by URIs. The assigned URN is urn:ietf:params:xml:rdfschema:<id>.

The RFC recommends looking at RFC 3151 as a method for minting a URN that can also be represented as a Formal Public Identifier.
sections.eli5: There are four shelves in the notebook: one for public labels, one for namespace names, one for schema files and one for RDF schemas. Each shelf has its own style of name tag.

sections.title: How to Register
sections.content:
Until IANA asks for or builds an automated process, a specification must make the request in the IANA considerations section of its own document, using a template with three fields.

  • URI: the URI or PUBLIC identifier for the XML component. To have IANA pick one, write "please assign".
  • Registrant Contact: the person or organization responsible, ideally with physical and network contact information. For standards developed in the IETF, the registrant is the IESG.
  • XML: the exact XML to store in the registry. Unless the start and end of the file are obvious, the document should mark them with the text "BEGIN" and "END". IANA inserts the text between them, minus page breaks and RFC formatting, into the file kept in the repository.
sections.eli5: To get into the notebook you fill in a small form with the name you want, who to call about it, and the exact text to keep. Then the librarian copies it in.

sections.title: Registry Policy and the New URN Sub-namespace
sections.content:
The RFC admits that it creates a rather large registry and that the effort to maintain it, and the policies around any approval process, are not trivial. The registry operates on a First Come First Served basis, but a Specification is Required. The text adds that these policies may change once the IETF has some experience with the registry.

Because RFC 3553 requires any new registry that needs a name under the urn:ietf:params namespace to describe its structure in template form, the RFC fills in that template. The registry name is xml, the specification is this document, the namespace is organized with one sub-namespace which is the <id>, and the index value is the class name.
sections.eli5: The rule is simple: first to ask gets the name, but you must have written down what it means. The RFC also tells the big URN office where the new shelf lives.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The information IANA maintains will be authoritative and so will be a target for attack. For some content, such as XML Schemas and DTDs, what IANA holds may be fed directly into software. The RFC therefore asks IANA to take extra care with security, as for any important reference location for the Internet.

Beyond that, it says there are no security considerations not already found with any other IANA registry.
sections.eli5: If everyone trusts the notebook, a bad guy would love to scribble in it. So the librarian has to guard it well.
